research_text:
## 1. API and finding

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents an implementation of a secure socket protocol. It is a factory for secure socket factories and `SSLEngine` instances, and can be initialized with key managers, trust managers, and a source of randomness. The reported finding concerns the **static, zero-argument call** `SSLContext.getDefault()`, not a negotiated TLS version. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Oracle documents `getDefault()` as returning a previously set default context or, on first use otherwise, obtaining one through `getInstance("Default")`. The returned default context is immediately usable without initialization. Oracle does **not** document the call itself as forbidden; that prohibition comes from the supplied CrySL rule. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Oracle API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html

## 2. Documented usage and remediation

Oracle documents `getInstance(protocol)` as selecting an implementation from registered providers and `init(km, tm, random)` as initializing a context. Any of those three initialization arguments may be `null`: provider-selected factories are used for null manager arrays, and the default randomness implementation is used for null randomness. This API-valid usage is distinct from the CrySL rule’s required manager and randomness predicates. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

For raw `SSLSocket` and `SSLEngine` use, Oracle says applications must verify peer credentials; those classes do not automatically check that the hostname matches the peer’s credentials. Endpoint identification can be performed during the handshake. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?source=%3Aow%3Alp%3Acpo%3A%3A&utm_source=openai))

Oracle’s documentation reviewed here gives **no general recommendation to replace `getDefault()`**, which it expressly supports. The CrySL rule identifies `Get`—its `getInstance` events—as the alternative to the forbidden call, but also imposes initialization, ordering, and predicate requirements. That is a **rule-specific alternative**, not an Oracle-prescribed universal remediation. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

Oracle JSSE guide: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html

## 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Protocol selection and wire behavior:** An `SSLContext` algorithm name is not itself the negotiated protocol. Oracle says even version-named contexts may support other SSL/TLS versions. Enabled protocols, provider defaults, disabled-algorithm settings, and the peer affect what can be negotiated. In particular, `getInstance("TLS")` alone does not establish that a legacy protocol is negotiated. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))
- **TLS 1.3 migration:** Oracle documents compatibility risks involving closure behavior, certificate signature algorithms, cipher suites, session resumption, and key updates. Thus a context change that changes actual enabled or negotiated versions can affect interoperability; the call replacement alone does not establish what happens on the wire. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/jsse/JSSERefGuide.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Platform support:** Java SE 21 requires implementations to support the `TLSv1.2` context algorithm; other support depends on the implementation. Oracle documents TLS 1.3 in JDK 11 and in JDK 8u261 and later. These statements do not establish support for every vendor, provider, or older update. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Persisted formats:** The reviewed `SSLContext` and CrySL sources do not document a persisted-format conversion or migration path for changing this call. They therefore do not establish whether any application-specific stored material needs migration.

Standard algorithm names: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html  
Oracle JDK 8 JSSE guide: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/jsse/JSSERefGuide.html

## 4. Exact CrySL rule

The supplied source declares `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`. Its matching clause is, verbatim: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

```crysl
FORBIDDEN
	getDefault() => Get;
```

The forbidden declaration names **`getDefault` with an empty parameter list** on the specified `SSLContext` type. It is not a name-only wildcard over arbitrary receiver types: a method that merely shares the name on an unrelated type is **not specified by this rule**. The call is static, so it has no instance receiver. The clause has no further value or runtime condition; it declares the call forbidden and points to `Get` as an alternative. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

Separately, the source defines `Get` as one- or two-argument `getInstance` calls, constrains their `protocol` value to `TLSv1.2` or `TLSv1.3`, and specifies `Get, Init, Engine?` plus the listed initialization predicates. That literal constraint is **not** a test of enabled or negotiated protocols. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

Rule source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl

**Source limits:** The URL points to a mutable branch. The supplied SHA-256 was not independently verified in this research pass, and the source alone does not establish the exact compiled rule artifact or detector implementation used for the reported finding.
